lesson.subtitle: Lesson 7 -- Defining What Matters
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Ana Paula Teodoro Valdivia | Lesson 7 -- Defining What Matters

listenings.text: I am not a lawyer, and I want to describe what actually happens to me on those calls. Our counsel is talking, everything is fine, and then she says force majeure. And I stop. Not because I am lost, but because some part of my brain goes looking for what that phrase means. I know I have heard it before. I think it is about something nobody can control. And while I am down there looking, she has said two more sentences, and I have heard none of them. Ten seconds, maybe fifteen. The problem is that the two sentences I lose are almost always the important ones, because the technical term usually comes right before the point. And I never interrupt. I am the manager. Asking what a word means in front of eight people feels like admitting I should not be in the room. So I write it down, I look it up later, and she leaves that call believing I followed her. She has no idea that she lost me at minute four.

For years I thought that simplifying was the same as losing precision. If I explained a concept in ordinary words, I was being sloppy, and somebody would catch me. Then I watched a senior partner in a board meeting. Somebody asked about severability, and he said: it is the rule that keeps the rest of the contract alive if one clause fails. Nine words. Nobody stopped him, nobody looked confused, and the meeting moved on. Nothing was lost. So I copied his habit, and it is the only writing rule I have kept. Before I send an opinion, I go through it and I find every technical term. For each one I write a definition of a single line, and then I do not put it in a footnote and I do not open a bracket. I fold it into the sentence with a relative clause. The term arrives and the meaning arrives with it, in the same breath. My opinions are not longer. They are just readable by the people who have to act on them.

extra_audio.text: Clause eleven deals with force majeure, which means an event nobody can control. It also lists the milestones that the supplier has to reach. The annex, which is attached at the end, has the full list of deliverables. So the board only has to read two pages, not forty.
